chapter.name: Salient Features of the Constitution
chapter.blurb: The main features of the Indian Constitution, its sources, and the criticisms made of it.

concepts.name: Lengthiest written constitution and its sources
concepts.description: The size of the Constitution, why it is so long, and the countries and Acts from which its features were drawn.
concepts.idea: India has the longest written constitution, made by drawing on many sources, chiefly the 1935 Act.
concepts.rule: The Constitution as adopted in 1949 had a Preamble, 395 Articles in 22 Parts and 8 Schedules. Today it has a Preamble, about 470 Articles in 25 Parts and 12 Schedules. Amendments since 1951 deleted about 20 Articles and one Part and added about 95 Articles, four Parts (IVA, IXA, IXB, XIVA) and four Schedules (9, 10, 11, 12). Four factors explain its size: the size and diversity of the country, the influence of the bulky 1935 Act, a single Constitution for both the Centre and states, and the dominance of legal experts in the Assembly. The 42nd Amendment (1976) is called the 'Mini-Constitution'. In 2019, Jammu and Kashmir lost its special status under Article 370 and was split into two Union territories, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. Ambedkar said it was framed after ransacking all known constitutions. The structure is largely from the 1935 Act; the philosophical part (Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles) draws on American and Irish sources respectively; the political part (cabinet government) comes from Britain. Other features come from Canada, Australia, Germany, the USSR, France, South Africa and Japan.
concepts.example: The federal scheme, governors, emergency powers and public service commissions were drawn from the 1935 Act.

concepts.name: Rigidity with flexibility and a federal system with a unitary bias
concepts.description: How Article 368 mixes amendment methods, and how India is federal in form but unitary in spirit.
concepts.idea: The Constitution blends rigid and flexible amendment and is a federation with a strong Centre.
concepts.rule: Article 368 provides two kinds of amendment: some provisions need a special majority of Parliament, meaning two-thirds of the members of each House present and voting and a majority of the total membership; others also need ratification by half of the states. Some provisions can be amended by a simple majority like ordinary laws and these do not come under Article 368. So the Constitution is a synthesis of rigidity and flexibility. It has the federal features of two governments, division of powers, written and supreme Constitution, rigidity, independent judiciary and bicameralism. It also has unitary features: a strong Centre, single Constitution, single citizenship, flexibility, integrated judiciary, Governors appointed by the Centre, all-India services and emergency provisions. The word 'Federation' is not used; Article 1 calls India a Union of States, meaning the federation is not the result of an agreement of states and no state can secede. It has been called quasi-federal (Wheare), bargaining federalism (Morris Jones), co-operative federalism (Granville Austin) and a federation with a centralising tendency (Ivor Jennings).
concepts.example: Article 1 describes India as a 'Union of States'.

concepts.name: Parliamentary government, sovereignty and judicial supremacy, and the integrated judiciary
concepts.description: The Westminster model in India, the balance between parliamentary sovereignty and judicial review, and the single hierarchy of courts.
concepts.idea: India follows the parliamentary system, balances Parliament and courts, and has one integrated, independent judiciary.
concepts.rule: India chose the British parliamentary system over the American presidential one. It rests on co-operation and coordination between the legislature and executive, and is called the Westminster model, responsible government or cabinet government. It exists at the Centre and in states. Features: nominal and real executives, majority party rule, collective responsibility, ministers being members of the legislature, leadership of the Prime Minister or Chief Minister and dissolution of the lower House. Unlike Britain, India's Parliament is not sovereign and the head of state is elected. The framers balanced British parliamentary sovereignty with American judicial supremacy: the Supreme Court can strike down laws through judicial review, while Parliament can amend most of the Constitution. India's judicial review is narrower because of 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 rather than 'due process of law'. The judiciary is integrated: the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts and subordinate courts below, enforcing both Central and state laws. Independence is protected by security of tenure, fixed service conditions, expenses charged to the Consolidated Fund, bar on discussing judges' conduct in the legislatures, ban on practice after retirement, the power to punish for contempt and separation from the executive.
concepts.example: The Supreme Court is the highest court of appeal and the guardian of the Constitution.

concepts.name: Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, Fundamental Duties and the secular State
concepts.description: The three sets of individual and State obligations and the secular character of the State.
concepts.idea: Rights protect citizens against State power, directives guide the State, duties remind citizens, and the State is secular.
concepts.rule: Part III guarantees six fundamental rights: equality (Articles 14-18), freedom (19-22), against exploitation (23-24), freedom of religion (25-28), cultural and educational rights (29-30) and constitutional remedies (32). The seventh, the right to property (Article 31), was deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is a legal right under Article 300A. Rights are justiciable, subject to reasonable restrictions, can be curtailed by amendment, and can be suspended in a national emergency except Articles 20 and 21. The Directive Principles in Part IV are a 'novel feature' according to Ambedkar, are socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual, are non-justiciable and aim at a welfare state, with public opinion as their real sanction. In Minerva Mills (1980) the Court said the Constitution rests on a balance between rights and directives. The Fundamental Duties, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation, sit in Part IVA (Article 51A); the 86th Amendment (2002) added the eleventh. The State is secular: 'secular' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment, and Articles 14 to 16, 25 to 30 and 44 reflect this. India follows the positive concept of secularism, equal respect for all religions.

concepts.name: Adult franchise, single citizenship, independent bodies, emergency provisions, three-tier and co-operative government
concepts.description: Further salient features: universal adult franchise, one citizenship, independent bodies, three types of emergency, local government and co-operative societies.
concepts.idea: The Constitution has universal adult franchise, one citizenship, independent bodies, emergency powers and three tiers of government.
concepts.rule: Universal adult franchise is the basis of elections to the Lok Sabha and state assemblies; every citizen aged 18 and over may vote without discrimination. The voting age was lowered from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment (1988), effective 1989. Though federal, India has a single citizenship, unlike the USA where a person is a citizen of both the nation and the state. The Constitution creates independent bodies: the Election Commission, the Comptroller and Auditor-General, the Union Public Service Commission and State Public Service Commissions. There are three types of emergency: national (Article 352, war, external aggression or armed rebellion), state emergency or President's Rule (Article 356 or 365) and financial (Article 360); in an emergency the federal structure works as a unitary one. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) added a third tier: Part IX and the 11th Schedule for panchayats and Part IXA and the 12th Schedule for municipalities (nagar panchayat, municipal council, municipal corporation). The 97th Amendment (2011) gave constitutional status to co-operative societies: it made forming them a fundamental right under Article 19, added Article 43B as a directive principle and inserted Part IXB.
concepts.example: The 73rd Amendment added Part IX and the 11th Schedule to the Constitution.

concepts.name: Criticism of the Constitution
concepts.description: Charges that it is borrowed, a copy of the 1935 Act, un-Indian, un-Gandhian, elephantine and a lawyers' paradise, and the replies.
concepts.idea: Critics called the Constitution a borrowed, bulky and un-Gandhian document, and Ambedkar answered them.
concepts.rule: Critics called the Constitution a 'borrowed Constitution', 'bag of borrowings' or 'hotch-potch'. Ambedkar replied that the framers modified borrowed features to suit Indian conditions and remove faults, and that a Constitution framed so late in history could only vary to fit needs. Critics also called it a 'carbon copy' of the 1935 Act, as N. Srinivasan, Ivor Jennings and P.R. Deshmukh said. Ambedkar replied that there was nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing and that no one holds patent rights on fundamental ideas, though he regretted that the borrowed provisions mostly concerned administration details. Others called it 'un-Indian or anti-Indian': K. Hanumanthaiya said they wanted the music of the veena or sitar but got the music of an English band. It was called 'un-Gandhian' as it was not built on village and district panchayats. It was called 'elephantine' by Ivor Jennings and H.V. Kamath, and a 'paradise of lawyers' by Jennings and H.K. Maheswari.
concepts.example: Ivor Jennings called the Constitution a 'lawyer's paradise'.
